title: Axe 1 : Identités et échanges - Identities and Exchanges
content: This thematic axis explores how individuals and communities shape their identities through exchanges and interactions. Key concepts include: cultural identity (heritage, traditions, values), migration and diaspora (immigration, emigration, cultural mixing), globalisation (cultural exchanges, homogenisation vs diversity), multicultural societies (integration, assimilation, multiculturalism), generational identities (youth culture, generation gap). Students analyse how identity is constructed through language, culture, history and social interactions. They examine how exchanges between different cultures can both enrich and challenge identities. Related vocabulary: heritage, roots, belonging, diversity, melting pot, acculturation, cross-cultural, expatriate, bilingualism.
typical_questions: How does migration affect cultural identity?
What are the benefits and challenges of multicultural societies?
common_errors: Oversimplifying identity as fixed rather than evolving

title: Axe 2 : Espace privé et espace public - Private and Public Spheres
content: This axis examines the boundaries between private life and public life in English-speaking societies. Key topics include: privacy and surveillance (CCTV, data protection, social media), freedom of expression (press freedom, censorship, whistleblowers), celebrities and public figures (media intrusion, public interest), architecture and urban planning (public spaces, gentrification), digital privacy (cookies, data mining, right to be forgotten). Students analyse how technology blurs the line between private and public, and how different cultures define these boundaries. They study texts about whistleblowers (Snowden, Assange), social media's impact on privacy, and the balance between security and individual rights.
typical_questions: Is privacy becoming obsolete in the digital age?
Should there be limits to freedom of expression?
common_errors: Ignoring cultural differences in privacy expectations

title: Axe 3 : Art et pouvoir - Art and Power
content: This axis explores the relationship between artistic expression and political power. Topics include: propaganda and art (wartime posters, political murals, totalitarian art), protest art and music (civil rights, punk, street art), censorship and artistic freedom (banned books, controversial artworks), art as soft power (cultural diplomacy, Hollywood), architecture and power (monuments, memorials, iconic buildings). Students analyse how art can serve, challenge or subvert power. They study examples like Banksy's street art, the Harlem Renaissance, protest songs from the 60s, and contemporary political art. Key vocabulary: propaganda, subversion, censorship, commissioned art, patronage, iconoclasm, counterculture.
typical_questions: Can art change society?
How do governments use art for propaganda?
common_errors: Seeing art as purely aesthetic without political dimensions

title: Axe 4 : Citoyenneté et mondes virtuels
content: This axis examines how digital technology transforms citizenship and civic engagement. Key themes: online activism and hacktivism (Anonymous, online petitions, social media campaigns), fake news and misinformation (fact-checking, media literacy), digital democracy (e-voting, online consultations, government transparency), virtual communities (gaming communities, online forums, digital identities), cyber-citizenship (netiquette, digital footprint, online harassment). Students analyse how technology enables new forms of political participation while creating new challenges for democracy. They examine case studies like the Arab Spring, Black Lives Matter, and Brexit campaign strategies.
typical_questions: How has social media changed political engagement?
Can online activism be as effective as traditional activism?
common_errors: Idealising online activism without seeing its limitations
Dismissing all online information as unreliable

title: Axe 5 : Fictions et réalités - Fictions and Realities
content: This axis explores the interplay between fiction and reality in English-speaking cultures. Topics include: utopias and dystopias (1984, Brave New World, The Handmaid's Tale), science fiction and technology (AI, space exploration, transhumanism), fake news and post-truth (alternative facts, conspiracy theories), reality TV and docudramas (authenticity, manipulation), virtual and augmented reality (gaming, simulation, metaverse). Students analyse how fiction reflects and shapes our understanding of reality. They study how dystopian literature warns about societal trends, how media blurs fact and fiction, and how new technologies create alternate realities.
typical_questions: What can dystopian fiction teach us about our society?
How do we distinguish fact from fiction in the digital age?
common_errors: Treating fiction as pure escapism without social commentary
Dismissing science fiction predictions as impossible

title: Axe 6 : Innovations scientifiques
content: This axis examines scientific and technological innovations in English-speaking countries. Key topics: medical breakthroughs (vaccines, gene therapy, stem cells), environmental technology (renewable energy, carbon capture, sustainable solutions), artificial intelligence (machine learning, automation, ethical concerns), space exploration (NASA, SpaceX, Mars colonisation), biotechnology (GMOs, cloning, CRISPR). Students analyse the benefits, risks and ethical implications of scientific progress. They study debates around climate technology, medical ethics, AI regulation, and the role of private companies in space. Key vocabulary: breakthrough, cutting-edge, trial, patent, ethics, sustainable, renewable.
typical_questions: Should there be ethical limits to scientific research?
Can technology solve the climate crisis?
common_errors: Being uncritically optimistic or pessimistic about technology
Ignoring the social and economic context of innovation

title: Axe 7 : Diversité et inclusion
content: This axis explores diversity and inclusion issues in English-speaking societies. Topics include: racial equality (civil rights movement, BLM, systemic racism), gender equality (feminism, gender pay gap, #MeToo), LGBTQ+ rights (marriage equality, Pride, transgender rights), disability rights (accessibility, representation, inclusive design), religious and cultural diversity (Islamophobia, antisemitism, cultural appropriation). Students analyse historical struggles and contemporary debates around equality and representation. They study key figures (Martin Luther King, Ruth Bader Ginsburg), landmark legislation (Civil Rights Act, Equality Act), and ongoing challenges in achieving true inclusion.
typical_questions: Has the civil rights movement achieved its goals?
What is the difference between equality and equity?
common_errors: Confusing equality with treating everyone identically

title: Axe 8 : Territoire et mémoire
content: This axis explores how territory shapes collective memory and identity. Topics include: colonial legacy (British Empire, Commonwealth, decolonisation), indigenous peoples (Native Americans, Aboriginal Australians, Māori), memorials and memory (war memorials, statues controversies, museums), borders and migration (Brexit, US-Mexico border, refugee crises), national parks and heritage sites (conservation, tourism, cultural significance). Students analyse how places carry historical meaning and how societies choose what to remember. They examine debates around Confederate statues, indigenous land rights, and the repatriation of cultural artefacts.
typical_questions: Should colonial statues be removed?
How do we reconcile with difficult histories?
common_errors: Ignoring indigenous perspectives on land and memory

title: Present Perfect : formation et emplois
content: The Present Perfect connects the past to the present. Formation: have/has + past participle (I have worked, she has gone). Key uses: 1) Life experience without specific time (I have visited Paris), 2) Recent past with present relevance (I have just finished), 3) Unfinished time periods (I have seen three films this week), 4) Duration from past to present with for/since (I have lived here for 5 years / since 2019). Time markers: just, already, yet, ever, never, recently, so far, up to now. Contrast with Simple Past: Simple Past = finished action at specific time (I visited Paris in 2020); Present Perfect = no specific time or connection to present. British vs American: British prefers Present Perfect for recent past (I've just eaten); American often uses Simple Past (I just ate).
typical_questions: When do we use Present Perfect instead of Simple Past?
What's the difference between 'for' and 'since'?
common_errors: Using Present Perfect with specific past time markers
Using Simple Past for unfinished time periods

title: Les modaux : can, could, may, might, must, should
content: Modal verbs express ability, possibility, permission, obligation or advice. Key modals: CAN (ability: I can swim; permission: Can I go?; possibility: It can be cold). COULD (past ability: I could run fast; polite request: Could you help?; possibility: It could rain). MAY (permission: May I leave?; possibility: It may rain). MIGHT (lower possibility: It might rain). MUST (strong obligation: You must wear a seatbelt; logical deduction: He must be tired). SHOULD (advice: You should see a doctor; expectation: She should arrive soon). Modals have no -s for third person, no infinitive, and are followed by bare infinitive. For past: could have + PP (possibility), should have + PP (regret), must have + PP (deduction). Mustn't = prohibition; don't have to = no obligation.
typical_questions: What's the difference between must and have to?
When do we use may vs might?
common_errors: Confusing mustn't and don't have to
Using 'can' in formal contexts where 'may' is better

title: Les conditionnels : 0, 1, 2, 3
content: Conditional sentences express hypothetical situations and their consequences. Type 0 (general truths): If + present, present (If you heat water, it boils). Type 1 (real/likely future): If + present, will + infinitive (If it rains, I will stay home). Type 2 (unreal present/unlikely): If + past simple, would + infinitive (If I won the lottery, I would travel). Type 3 (unreal past/impossible): If + past perfect, would have + PP (If I had studied, I would have passed). Mixed conditionals combine types: If I had taken the job [past unreal], I would be rich now [present result]. Unless = if not. Key: Type 2 uses 'were' for all subjects in formal English (If I were you). Wish + past = present regret; wish + past perfect = past regret.
typical_questions: When do we use the second conditional?
What's the difference between Type 2 and Type 3?
common_errors: Using 'was' instead of 'were' in formal Type 2

title: Reported Speech : discours indirect
content: Reported speech conveys what someone said without quoting directly. Key changes: 1) Tense backshift: present → past ("I am" → he said he was), will → would, can → could. 2) Pronouns: I → he/she, you → I/he, my → his/her. 3) Time/place: today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, here → there, this → that. Reporting verbs: say, tell (+ object), ask, explain, admit, deny, suggest, promise, warn. Questions: "Where are you going?" → She asked where I was going (no inversion, no question mark). Commands: "Sit down" → She told me to sit down. No backshift needed if: the statement is still true, the reporting verb is present tense. Suggest + gerund or that + subjunctive (She suggested going / that we go).
typical_questions: How do tenses change in reported speech?
What's the difference between say and tell?
common_errors: Using question word order in reported questions

title: La voix passive en anglais
content: The passive voice shifts focus from the doer to the receiver of the action. Formation: be + past participle. Active: The company employs 500 people. Passive: 500 people are employed (by the company). Tenses: Present simple (is/are made), past simple (was/were made), present perfect (has/have been made), future (will be made), modal (can be made, must be done). Uses: 1) Unknown agent (My car was stolen), 2) Unimportant agent (The bridge was built in 1900), 3) Formal/scientific writing (The experiment was conducted), 4) Avoiding blame (Mistakes were made). By + agent is optional. Some verbs have two passives: They gave him a prize → He was given a prize / A prize was given to him. Impersonal passive: It is said that... / He is said to be...
typical_questions: When should we use the passive voice?
How do we form the passive in different tenses?
common_errors: Using passive when active is clearer
Forgetting to change the verb to past participle

title: L'expression de l'opinion et l'argumentation
content: Expressing opinions and building arguments requires varied vocabulary and structures. Giving opinions: In my view/opinion, I believe/think/feel that, It seems to me that, As far as I'm concerned, From my point of view. Agreeing: I totally agree, That's a good point, You're absolutely right, I couldn't agree more. Disagreeing: I'm not sure I agree, I see it differently, I take your point but, With respect, I disagree. Adding arguments: Furthermore, Moreover, In addition, What's more. Contrasting: However, Nevertheless, On the other hand, Although, Despite. Concluding: To sum up, In conclusion, All things considered, On balance. Structure: Introduction (state position), Body (arguments + examples + counterarguments), Conclusion (restate + final thought). Use hedging (tend to, may, might, generally) to avoid over-generalisation.
typical_questions: How do I structure an argumentative essay?
What phrases can I use to express disagreement politely?

title: La compréhension orale : stratégies d'écoute
content: Effective listening comprehension requires active strategies. Before listening: read questions carefully, predict content from context/title, identify key information needed. During first listen: focus on global understanding (who, what, where, when, why), note key words, don't panic at unknown words. During second listen: focus on details, verify predictions, complete answers. Key strategies: context clues (background noise, tone), discourse markers (firstly, however, in conclusion), stressed words carry meaning, connected speech (gonna, wanna, dunno). Common accents: British RP, American, Australian, Scottish, Indian English. Practice with various sources: news (BBC, CNN), podcasts, TED talks, films, songs. Note-taking tips: use abbreviations, symbols, focus on content words. Improve by: regular exposure, active listening, repeating/shadowing, transcribing.

What should I focus on during a listening exam?

title: L'expression orale : interaction et présentation
content: Oral expression in English requires fluency, accuracy and communicative strategies. For presentations: structure clearly (introduction, body, conclusion), use signposting (I'll start by, Moving on to, To conclude), maintain eye contact, vary intonation, use visually supporting materials. For interaction: active listening, asking clarification questions (Could you explain...? What do you mean by...?), turn-taking, agreeing/disagreeing politely, building on others' ideas. Pronunciation tips: word stress (PHOtograph vs phoTOGrapher), sentence stress (content words), intonation (rising for questions, falling for statements), connected speech. Fillers: Well, Actually, I mean, You know (use sparingly). Handling difficulties: paraphrasing when lacking vocabulary, asking for repetition (Sorry, could you say that again?), self-correction. Practice: record yourself, get feedback, participate in conversations, shadow native speakers.
typical_questions: How can I improve my English speaking?
What makes a good oral presentation?
common_errors: Reading from notes instead of speaking naturally

title: False friends : les faux-amis anglais-français
content: False friends (faux-amis) are words that look similar in French and English but have different meanings. Common false friends: actually = en fait (not actuellement = currently), eventually = finalement (not éventuellement = possibly), sensible = raisonnable (not sensible = sensitive), library = bibliothèque (not librairie = bookshop), journey = voyage (not journée = day), résumé = CV (not résumé = summary), lecture = cours magistral (not lecture = reading), location = emplacement (not location = rental), sympathetic = compatissant (not sympathique = nice), attend = assister à (not attendre = wait), demand = exiger (not demander = ask), achieve = accomplir (not achever = finish), ancient = antique (not ancien = former), coin = pièce de monnaie (not coin = corner), properly = correctement (not proprement = cleanly). Always verify meanings in context and use a good dictionary.
